scenes.script_line: If you are going to represent Craveiral, you have to know Craveiral the way you know your own home. This module is a visit, and it has two parts: the facts, and the standard. The facts, because confidence sells and vagueness kills. The standard, because a house made ready is not a clean room — it is a promise kept. We start with the facts.

scenes.script_line: Thirty-eight independent houses, organised in clusters — three main clusters plus the Studios, closer to the central services. They share the same DNA: sustainability, local craft, a nod to Portuguese heritage. Minimal, but warm. Every unit has a properly equipped kitchen, organic amenities, air conditioning, and a private terrace with table and armchairs. And pets are welcome — which matters to more guests every year, and which we do properly, not grudgingly.

scenes.script_line: The typologies, and these you should know by heart. Studios: forty square metres, two guests. Farm Houses: sixty-four metres, one bedroom, up to four. Farm Lofts: also sixty-four metres, two guests, WeWood interiors in cherry and oak, in the Cravo cluster — which has a private pool for its guests. Two-bedroom houses: eighty-five metres, four in comfort, up to six, wood burner in the living room. Farmers House: two bedrooms, Dam furniture, Smeg kitchen, two decks. And the Owner's House WeWood: our signature — eighty-five metres, Hästens mattress, cork bathtub, a small library.

scenes.script_line: Why do we make you learn square metres? Because of this situation. A guest asks: “does the two-bedroom house work for us with the children?” Two answers are possible. The vague one — “yes, I think so” — leaves the guest where they were. The precise one: “yes, and if they are small the sofa bed in the living room gives you room to spare; the second bedroom can be twins or a double, tell me which you prefer.” That answer has just built trust. And trust is the currency of this business.

scenes.script_line: The shared spaces, half of what the guest is buying. Three pools: the big outdoor one, twenty-four by nine metres, for real swimming; the heated indoor, twelve by five, with the glass-fronted sauna beside it; and the children's pool. The wellness deck, raised in the pine wood: outdoor sauna, hot tub, cold plunge — a full thermal circuit. The gym. The Nature Interpretation Center, wood and glass among the pines: yoga twice a week, retreats, workshops, meetings; fifty seated for a banquet, eighty standing. The terrace with the fire pits. And the playground area, for events up to three hundred people.

scenes.script_line: Now the standard, and here the tone changes. A standard is a promise we made to every future guest, based on what we delivered to the past ones. The guest paid for the Craveiral of the photographs and the reviews. Every detail right keeps that promise: the flawless bed, the kitchen without a mark, the inviting terrace, the amenities complete. Every detail wrong breaks it a little. Broken promises pile up in silence: guests rarely complain about small things — they think less of us quietly, book elsewhere one day, and we never know why.

No people, no text. | [ARCHIVE] 11s Sequence of details done right: amenities aligned, jug filled, terrace cushion dry. | [GRAPHICS] 10s Visual counter: promises kept adding up, one failing.

scenes.script_line: Hence the rule I want you to keep: details are not small. Here, details are everything, because our whole promise is care. A farm that preaches love of the land and has a dirty pool filter or a dead bulb on a boardwalk is a contradiction the guest feels at once, even if they cannot explain it. Coherence between what we say and what we do is our highest standard. And one thing only guest wellbeing asks for gets forgotten: sleep. Total blackout, maintenance noise at an agreed hour, never knocking before ten in the morning unless asked.
scenes.visual_direction: [GENERATE] 6s PROMPT: A single dead lightbulb on a weathered wooden post at dusk, unlit while others glow further down the path. Slow push in. Blue-hour light. Palette: dusk blue, warm amber, brown. 6 seconds. Generic rural walkway, no identifiable buildings, no text. | [ARCHIVE] 10s Maintenance working early, discreetly. | [ARCHIVE] 10s Bedroom in full darkness, curtain closing. | [GRAPHICS] 11s Three sleep rules on short cards.
scenes.onscreen: Details are not small. · then: Blackout · Noise by appointment · Never before 10

scenes.script_line: Last point, and a test of character. When you see something wrong that is not “your job” — a fallen branch on the boardwalk, a dirty window, litter by the pool — there are two kinds of people. The one who thinks “someone should sort that out”, and the one who sorts it or reports it within the hour. Craveiral was built by the second kind. Be the second kind. Next module: the FarmTable — where all this philosophy lands.
scenes.visual_direction: [GENERATE] 7s PROMPT: A fallen pine branch lying across a wooden boardwalk. A pair of work-worn hands enters frame, lifts it, carries it out of frame. No faces, generic rural setting. Handheld, slight movement. Warm morning light. Palette: sand, pine green, brown. 7 seconds. No text. | [GRAPHICS] 12s Split: “someone should sort that out” fading / “within the hour” locking in terracotta. | [ARCHIVE] 14s Wide shot of the houses at end of day, music rising. | [GRAPHICS] 8s Belong close.
scenes.onscreen: Fix or report. Within the hour.
